sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Daidalos** (*daedalus*) — Craftsman, Inventor, Wings · Cunningly wrought — belongs to the Greek tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Craftsman, Inventor, Wings". The name means "Cunningly wrought"[^1].

**Daidalos** is the master craftsman of Greek mythology: the architect of the Labyrinth, the maker of moving statues, and the father of Icarus. His name means "cunningly wrought" and became a byword for any work so skillful that it seemed alive. He is the first engineer in Western literature, the inventor whose ingenuity saves him and destroys those he loves.[^2]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Daidalos** and serves its temple at [its temple](https://punicodex.com/daedalus/). The original carries both stress and vowel length, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1. The plain ASCII form *daedalus* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The name is attested in Greek as **Δαίδαλος**. Etymologically it means "Cunningly wrought"[^1].

The ASCII form *daedalus* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Daidalos** recovers the full diacritic detail of the scholarly transliteration directly in the address bar. The original carries both stress and vowel length, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **d** → **D** — Same
- **a** → **a** — Same
- **e** → **i** — Iota
- **d** → **d** — Same
- **a** → **a** — Same
- **l** → **l** — Same
- **u** → **o** — Omicron
- **s** → **s** — Same

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/dai̯.da.los/** — Attic Greek Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **Dai-** — Long diphthong αι [ai̯] with acute pitch accent; the alpha is open and the iota forms an off-glide.
- **-da-** — Short [da], the middle syllable of the name.
- **-los** — Short [los], the final syllable with a clear liquid l.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'DIE-dah-los' — the first syllable is long and carries the ancient pitch rise; the remaining syllables are short and light.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Greek** — Δαίδαλος (Daidalos), the cunningly wrought craftsman
- **Latin** — Daedalus, the Roman rendering adopted into English

The Greek Δαίδαλος contains both stress (acute on the diphthong) and length (the diphthong αι is long), making it a Tier 1 restoration. The Latin-derived English form Daedalus is a secondary spelling that preserves the consonants but obscures the original Greek vowel quantities.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
The name is written in Greek as **Δαίδαλος**. This original script is the form against which the ASCII fallback *daedalus* and the PuniCodex restoration **Daidalos** are measured: the restoration preserves its full diacritic detail of the written form, so that a reader typing the modern address still speaks the ancient name.[^1]

The name is written in Greek as **Δαίδαλος**. The first syllable is a long diphthong αι with an acute accent. The plain ASCII *daedalus* flattens the diphthong into ae and removes the accent. The PuniCodex restoration **Daidalos** preserves the scholarly transliteration of the Greek form and is classified as Tier 1 because the diphthong is long and accented.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
**Daidalos** is the master craftsman of Greek mythology: the architect of the Labyrinth, the maker of moving statues, and the father of Icarus. His name means "cunningly wrought" and became a byword for any work so skillful that it seemed alive. He is the first engineer in Western literature, the inventor whose ingenuity saves him and destroys those he loves.[^1]

### The Labyrinth

The maze Daidalos built to contain the Minotaur at Knossos.

### Wings

The feathered wings he fashioned from wax and twine to escape Crete.

### Automata

The moving statues he made so lifelike that they had to be chained down.

### Invention

The transforming power of human skill, celebrated and feared by the Greeks.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The iconography associated with Daidalos concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:[^1]

- **Wings** — The instruments of escape and the boundary between human and divine.
- **Wax** — The material that holds the wings together and melts when Icarus flies too close to the sun.
- **Labyrinth** — The architectural puzzle that embodies Daidalos' cunning and its dangerous consequences.
- **Tools** — The axe, file, and compass of the craftsman who can make anything except a safe life.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The myths of Daidalos are preserved in Homer, the lost *Catalogue of Women*, Diodorus Siculus, Ovid, and Apollodorus. They celebrate the power of human invention and warn against its costs: jealousy, exile, and the death of a son.[^1]

### The Killing of Talos (Athens)

Daidalos was born in Athens, where his skill as an inventor aroused the jealousy of his nephew Talos (or Perdix). When the boy invented the saw and the potter's wheel, Daidalos threw him from the Acropolis in envy. For this murder he was exiled from Athens and fled to Crete, where King Minos welcomed him.[^2]

### The Labyrinth (Crete)

At Knossos, Daidalos built the Labyrinth to house the Minotaur, the half-man, half-bull born of Pasiphae. The maze was so cunningly designed that even its maker could barely find his way out. When Theseus came to slay the Minotaur, Ariadne gave him the thread that Daidalos had taught her to use.

### The Wings (Crete)

When Minos imprisoned Daidalos and his son Icarus in the Labyrinth, Daidalos made wings from feathers and wax. He warned Icarus not to fly too close to the sun, but the boy, exulting in flight, ignored him. The wax melted, Icarus fell into the sea, and Daidalos flew on alone to Sicily.

### Death of Daidalos (Sicily)

In Sicily, Daidalos built marvellous works for King Cocalus. When Minos came to demand his surrender, Cocalus' daughters killed Minos in his bath. Daidalos lived out his life in Sicily, still inventing, still exiled from the ordinary happiness of family and home.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
The Greek Daidalos was absorbed into Roman literature as Daedalus, most famously in Ovid's *Metamorphoses*. In the Renaissance he became an emblem of the artist as rebel and genius, and in modern culture he stands for every inventor who creates what he cannot control. James Joyce made Stephen Dedalus a Daidalos-figure, the young artist escaping the nets of family, religion, and nation. The name has also been used for spacecraft, engineering projects, and artificial-intelligence ventures.[^1]

Within the Greek tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[acheron|Achérōn]], [[achilleus|Achilleús]], [[adamas|Adámas]], [[aer|Aḗr]], [[aither|Aithḗr]], and [[ajax|Aias]].

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body: Daidalos is the archetype of the engineer, the artist, and the scientist whose creations escape his intentions. He built the Labyrinth, the wings, and the moving statues; each invention brought wonder and disaster. Modern discussions of artificial intelligence, genetic engineering, and autonomous weapons revisit his dilemma: can we make things so complex that even their makers cannot predict their effects? Daidalos reminds us that skill without wisdom is exile.[^1]

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
No monument, inscription, or artifact in the current PuniCodex corpus is yet assigned to Daidalos with certainty. That absence should be read honestly: for a Greek name of this type the material record is expected to be thin, and the primary evidence remains the textual testimony gathered in the Scholarly Sources section[^1].

Were such evidence to surface, it would take recognizable forms: votive or dedicatory inscriptions naming Δαίδαλος, sanctuary or cult remains tied to craftsman and iconography matching its traditional attributes (wings and wax). Each candidate would be weighed against the reconstructed form of the name before entering the scholarly record.

sections.label: Homeric Hymns
sections.body:
The Homeric Hymns, a collection of ancient Greek hexameter poems, include invocations and narratives that shape the reception of Daidalos. While Daidalos does not always receive a separate, surviving hymn, the figure appears in the broader epic and hymnic environment that celebrates the Olympian order.

The hymns map divine genealogy, power, and cultic honor, and Daidalos's role as craftsman places the name within that hexameter world. The PuniCodex restoration Daidalos preserves the prosodic features that rhapsodes would have articulated.[^1]
sections.editorNotes: Synthesized from canonical sources by PuniCodex Team.

sections.label: Epithets & Epicleses
sections.body:
Greek gods and heroes accumulate epithets — cultic titles that specify place, function, or quality. For Daidalos, the tradition preserves epithets that stress craftsman.

Epicleses connected with Wings, Wax, Labyrinth sharpen the name for local worship and literary invocation. The restored form Daidalos carries the same vowel quantities that these epithets inherited in oral performance.[^1]

sections.label: Oracle & Cult Sites
sections.body:
Sanctuaries and oracular centers anchored the cult of Daidalos in the Greek landscape. Major sites include locations where the domain of craftsman was ritually honored.

Pilgrims, offerings, and festival calendars tied the name to specific topography. The restoration Daidalos gives the figure a stable address in the digital landscape analogous to those ancient centers.[^1]

sections.label: Iconography
sections.body:
Vase painting, sculpture, and votive reliefs disseminate the visual identity of Daidalos. Artists returned to attributes such as Wings, Wax, Labyrinth, creating a recognizable iconographic shorthand.

The restored spelling Daidalos reproduces in text the same precision that painters sought in image. Each attribute encodes a claim about power, identity, or function.[^1]

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Daidalos is the first Western portrait of the inventor as tragic hero. His gifts are extraordinary; his judgement is not. He kills his nephew from envy, builds a prison for a monster, and loses his son to the very technology that saved him. Each invention solves one problem and creates another.

To meditate on Daidalos is to meditate on the double edge of human making. We are the species that makes wings, and we are the species whose children fly too high. The question is not whether to invent but whether we can invent with the humility that knows our limits.[^1]
